passage:
Afreen, head of the customer support department, had to bring in a new shift system. She could have simply announced it, but she called the team to the meeting room.
"This changes everyone's week," she said. "If you don't accept it, it won't work, so tell me what you think."
Tarun raised a point about late finishes and bus timings. Others asked about weekends. The meeting ran forty minutes over.
The next Monday she came back with a changed rota: shorter late shifts and alternate weekends. It took two weeks longer than announcing it would have, but the team accepted it and hardly anyone asked to swap.

qa.q: How long did the meeting run over?
qa.a: The meeting ran forty minutes over.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when she asked the team for their views?
qa.a: Afreen was probably concerned that the team would reject the change, since she said it won't work if they don't accept it.

qa.q: What could Afreen do if some staff still dislike the new rota?
qa.a: Afreen could hold a short review after a month and adjust the rota, since the team's acceptance decides whether it works.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel after the changed rota?
qa.a: Tarun raised the bus timings and saw shorter late shifts come back, so may feel listened to.

grounding: A department head consults her team about a new shift system since their acceptance decides whether it works, even if it takes longer.

passage:
"So that's the draft," Parveen said, turning the whiteboard toward the nine lab staff. "Two rotating shifts instead of fixed ones. Before I send it up, I want to hear what breaks."
Jasleen crossed her arms. "Madam, honestly? Rotating every week will be very hard for anyone with small kids."
"Say more."
"School drop-offs. If I'm on early one week and late the next, I can't plan anything with my mother-in-law."
Another technician called from the back, "And the last bus goes at ten."
Parveen wrote both on the board. "Okay. What if the rotation is monthly, not weekly? And we check the bus times before fixing the late shift?"
"Monthly I could manage," Jasleen said slowly.
"This will take two more weeks than I planned," Parveen admitted. "But if you all hate it, it won't work anyway. We meet again Friday."

qa.q: When does the last bus go?
qa.a: The last bus goes at ten.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when admitting the delay?
qa.a: Parveen seemed a little uneasy about losing two weeks, but calm and sure it was worth it, since the staff hating the plan would make it fail.

qa.q: What else could Parveen do before Friday?
qa.a: Parveen could check the bus times and quietly ask staff who didn't speak up, so the next draft reflects everyone and not just the loudest voices.

qa.q: How does Jasleen see being asked before the change?
qa.a: Jasleen feels able to speak honestly, and by the end is open to a monthly rotation, because the real problem was heard and written on the board.

grounding: Shows a department head asking her lab staff about a new shift pattern because their acceptance decides whether it works, even though it takes longer.

passage: When management asked me to bring in a new shift pattern for the front office, my first thought was to design it myself over a weekend. I know the numbers; I've done the rosters for three years. But I kept picturing the notice going up and twelve people reading it in silence, then quietly swapping duties among themselves. So I asked instead. I held two short meetings, one for the day staff and one at midnight for the night desk. Lakshmi, who has been at the hotel longer than I have, said, "Pallavi ma'am, nobody minds nights. They mind not knowing until Sunday which nights." That changed everything. The fix was publishing the roster two weeks ahead, not the pattern itself. It took a month instead of a weekend. The new roster started last week, and so far only one swap request has come in.

qa.q: How far ahead is the roster now published?
qa.a: The roster is published two weeks ahead.

qa.q: What was Pallavi worried might happen if the pattern was designed alone?
qa.a: Pallavi was worried the twelve staff would read the notice in silence and quietly swap duties among themselves, so the plan would fail without anyone saying so.

qa.q: Why might the slower approach work better than a weekend plan?
qa.a: Because the staff helped find the real problem, they are more likely to accept the roster, and the single swap request so far suggests it is working.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel about being asked?
qa.a: Lakshmi likely feels respected and trusted, able to point out the real issue: not knowing until Sunday which nights to work.

grounding: Shows a department head consulting the hotel's front-office staff before changing shifts because their acceptance decides whether it works, even though it took longer.
